questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I chose the destination South Korea, as i wanted to experience a culture and a country i didn't know. I chose it as it was an overseas destination, a non-english speaking country, and somewhere which i had never been. I also chose South Korea as the semester timewise aligns well with our semester at University of Copenhagen.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I loved it! Would recommend the experience!

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: I think it was easy. The most complicated thing was having to register for Alien Registration Card upon arrival. But the Korea University did a good job at informing us about the application process.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: We received assistance from the school itself as well as buddies. The buddies were very willing to help, if we had problems with anything also. I had some complications with borrowing books atthe library though. Here the global service center at Korea University was quick to reply but not really helpful.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: Mentioned above.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: It was easy to find a place. But the place I ended up staying was pretty bad.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: For South Korea they should know that many goshiwon's/goshitels (VERY small studio apartments) lie about the size and pictures of the room.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I would have picked dorms instead of off-campus housing if I had been certain to get a single room. However, they only have very few single rooms making this unlikely. This is why i opted for living off-campus.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I remember prior to actually being admitted it was SO hard to find courses for graduate students. In general the Korea University systems (at least those in English) are catered mostly towards undergrads. When we got to the registration it was pretty easy for me to get courses, but I also think my courses were not very popular. I heard of other students (especially within business and administration studies) getting in to almost no courses at the first try, as the courses were filled up within  seconds of opening. I was lucky, but one cannot be sure to attend the courses they wish at Korea University.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: Courses open at a specific date and time. You better b e ready to sign up for the courses right as they open, or you can be almost sure not to get into the course. There's an add/drop period at the first week of the semester, which was a saving grace for many students who did not get the courses they wanted in the beginning.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: I got luckily got admitted to my prioritized courses in the first try, so I don't know.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Successful (but lucky that i wanted unpopular courses). But I also got permission to attend to courses, which were originally unavailable for exchange students.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Be ready when registration opens. And do have a plan B, if you don't get your prioritized courses.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I loved the courses i attended. Though two of them are not normally available for exchange students.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: It was different. One course had a really heavy work load and i very high academic level. The others were also good but a bit more easy.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: One course was very similar, the two other very different. I had one course were the final was a memorization test, which is very unlikely and uncommon within humanistic disciplines (at least in Denmark).

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
MAC638 Film Theories
IKS316 Korean Cinema In A Global Context
IKS317 History Of Korean Art

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I would recommend all of these courses, however, the last two are normally not available for exchange students. The first one, which is available, has a very talented professor. She has a very engaging teaching style, and i learned so much during this course. But the workload is very heavy.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer:
You have to pay for NHI (National Health Insurance) even if you have travel insurance. It's not very expensive, but it is annoying. You also have to pay for applying for Alien Registration Card 
 (ARC). Phone plans are also quite expensive in South Korea, and you do need a Korean phone number to book an appointment for ARC. Otherwise most other things are cheaper in South Korea than in Denmark.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Phone plans are more expensive. If you plan to do any free time activity (i signed up for a yoga studio for instance), these can also be pretty expensive. Food is cheap! And you can live really cheap if you're willing to live in a very small space.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I wanted to try some of these out, but the information was pretty hard to find for exchange students and non-korean speakers. It seems though, that most clubs you have to sign up for in the spring semester. As i was there in the fall semester, some clubs were unavailable to sign up for. I think they had some interesting clubs, but the information  about them was not really presented to us.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There was a lot of dinners with your KUBA group (Korea University Buddies Assistants) in the beggining. They also made a trip to a theme park. There was an international students festival also, but I didn't go.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I signed up for a international yoga studio called the Flow Room. It was a it expensive but really nice. Even though there are many things to explore, it's important to make time for your usual hobbies .

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: To travel around South Korea when you have time, maybe just for weekend trips. There's so many other areas that are interesting to explore besides Seoul. Almost all exchange students made sure to visit Busan and Jeju Island, so save up for these trips! I also did a templestay for christmas, which was absolutely amazing, and not very expensive!

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: I had a pretty easy time adjusting, but I also love exploring foreign cultures, and did research in advance, so I didn't really experience culture shock.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: I mostly socialized with other exchange students.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Mostly that many things are hard to do without a Korean Phone no. and Alien Registration Card. You will get your ARC 2-3 months into your stay. You also need to make sure your phone plan offers official authentification. You need these to pay for anything online, order food, make appointments online for clinics and doctors, reservation for sports games, cultural events etc. This is a nuisance for a foreigner who has just arrived in South Korea

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: I think people were very talktative and open, which was really nice! It's easy to find someone to speak to. The food is also so delicious! I would recommend to both explore th traditional as well as the more modern aspects of Seoul, there's so muvh to learn and see! There's often interesting public events such as fireworks, lightshows and markets which were so much fun to attend!

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Sign up for courses the second course registration opens. But even if you don't make it here, know that you might still be able to change it in the add/drop period.
2. Ask if your phone plan offers official authentification before buying it.
3. Visit destinations outside of Seoul such as Busan and Jeju Island.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: If you do off-campus housing BE CRITICAL. They're not honest when it comes to pictures and size of rooms/apartments. But remember that probably won't spend so much time in your room anyway, as you're out experiencing South Korea and Seoul. So maybe it's okay to live small, as long as it's cheap.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Just to get to experience and live in a foreign culture. You are able to immerse into the experience differently than if you're just on vacation which is very rewarding.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: To sign up for things and make reservations withou a Korean Phone number (with official authentification) and Alien Registration Card.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer:
It's not as normal to do gap years in other countries as it is in Denmark, so depending on your age stage of your studies, you might experience quite an age gap. I'm a 25 year old graduate student, and most local students and exchange students are undergraduates, who has not done any gap years.

Also as most exchange are undergrads, in my experience the University sometimes "forgot" to deliver information to graduate students. For instance the course list for graduate students is difficult to find, and towards the end of the semester the Global Service Center forgot to add graduate students to the mailing list (meaning we had to ask for information regarding grading, transcripts etc. ourselves, while this information were automatically delivered to undergrads).

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
